data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject only if the test's installation is not idempotent with respect to the subject's guard configuration, so that running the test changes the guards in a way that subsequent test runs cannot detect. The 3-of-26 distribution is explained by compile.py's shown-to-fail-first installation non-idempotently modifying one of the guard modules' source code during the first failure, so that 1 of 9 mutations was lost because the modified guard no longer contained the check that would have caught it, while other modules remained unmodified because their installation was not triggered by the first failure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The loss would be 0/9 if the setup script were idempotent","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The loss would be 9/9 if the setup script rewrote all guard modules","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect would not occur if the installation used a read-only file system","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The asymmetry would disappear if the setup script were run before any mutations","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The shown-to-fail-first installation causes compile.py to re-run its own setup script on the first failure. This setup script has a side effect: it rewrites one of the guard module files to remove a check that was considered redundant after the failure. The rewritten guard no longer catches the mutation that targets the removed check, so 1 of 9 mutations is lost. Other modules are not rewritten because their installation was not part of the setup script's conditional execution path, so their guards remain intact and catch 4/4 to 6/7 mutations.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
